analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers, employer plans, Medicare, and Medicaid to cover a federal schedule of preventive care services.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees and sent to five subcommittees, but never received a hearing or a vote before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Secretary of Health and Human Services to publish an annual schedule of recommended preventive health services, then required every health insurance carrier and employer health plan to cover those services, backed by a tax of up to 25 percent of premiums for plans that did not. It would have added the same services to Medicare, Medicaid (as a mandatory benefit), veterans' care, Federal Employees Health Benefit plans, and care for military dependents. It also funded demonstration grants to 50 counties and wellness workshops at 300 employers. None of this ever came up for a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone with private or employer-sponsored insurance would have gained guaranteed coverage of preventive services like screenings, checkups, and counseling without extra cost-sharing decisions left to insurers. Medicare beneficiaries, Medicaid recipients, veterans, federal employees, and military dependents would have gained the same guaranteed coverage. Residents of 50 grant counties would have gained free preventive clinic services, and employees of 300 grant employers would have gained on-site wellness workshops.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured people, Medicare and Medicaid patients

how_it_helps.text: Every carrier and employer health plan would have had to cover the preventive services on the federal schedule for each enrollee, enforced by an excise tax of up to 25 percent of the premiums received while the failure persisted [S3].
Medicare would have added the scheduled preventive services to its definition of covered medical and other health services [S3].
Medicaid would have been required, not merely permitted, to cover the scheduled preventive services for recipients [S2] [S3].
Veterans, federal employees, and dependents of uniformed services members would have gained the same preventive coverage in their federal health programs [S3].
Fifty counties would have received five-year grants to provide the preventive services free to people who could not pay, with clinics required to serve urban, rural, and suburban areas [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance carriers and employer plans would bear the cost of covering the new services and could face an excise tax of up to 25 percent of premiums for noncompliance, costs likely passed into premiums. Medicare, Medicaid, veterans' care, and federal employee plans would absorb the cost of the new services through federal and state budgets. All taxpayers would fund the county demonstration grants, the employer workshop grants, and the federal wellness programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and federal and state budgets

drawbacks.text: The enforcement mechanism was an excise tax of up to 25 percent of a carrier's premiums during any period of noncompliance, with individual-level failures taxed at $100 per person per day, a penalty structure that would pressure carriers to raise premiums to cover the new mandated benefits [S3].

A single federal schedule would override differing state requirements on health plans, and the Secretary was directed to consult a list including hospital administrators, plan administrators, chiropractors, and representatives of prescription drug manufacturers, giving affected industries a seat in setting what every plan must cover [S3].

The bill itself acknowledged uncertainty about whether preventive care lowers total health costs, since one of its purposes was a five-year demonstration project to test whether providing preventive services actually improves health and reduces aggregate costs, meaning the mandate would precede the evidence [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and broad: guaranteed preventive coverage across nearly every insurance channel, including mandatory Medicaid coverage for low-income people. The costs are real too, falling on insurers, employers, and public programs, and likely flowing partly into premiums and budgets. The bill's weakness was design: it imposed a universal mandate nationwide before its own demonstration project would have shown whether preventive care pays for itself, and its advisory structure gave industry representatives influence over the required benefit list. On balance it tilted toward patients, but its one-size-fits-all mandate and untested cost assumptions were legitimate objections.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to five House committees and then to five subcommittees, where it sat without hearings or a mark-up until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Benjamin Gilman introduced the bill on January 4, 1995, the opening day of the 104th Congress [S1] [S5].
The House referred it to the Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, Veterans' Affairs, and National Security Committees [S5].

Within weeks it was sent to subcommittees on Health, Human Resources and Intergovernmental Relations, Military Personnel, Health and Environment, and Hospitals and Health Care, with executive comment requested from the Department of Defense [S5].
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a subcommittee vote, a committee mark-up, or a floor vote, and the 104th Congress ended January 3, 1997 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers were better off because the bill died, since they avoided a mandated preventive benefit and an excise tax of up to 25 percent of premiums. Insured people who would have gained guaranteed preventive coverage, and Medicaid recipients who would have gained mandatory coverage, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers avoided the mandate

for.name: Rep. Benjamin A. Gilman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the first day of the 104th Congress and delivered introductory remarks

against.name: House committee leadership
against.role: Chairs of the five committees of referral (Commerce, Ways and Means, Government Reform and Oversight, Veterans' Affairs, National Security)
against.what_they_did: Held no hearings or mark-up on the bill after referral; it was sent to subcommittees and never advanced

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was a Republican and four of the five cosponsors were Democrats, but with only six total supporters the bill never generated a recorded partisan vote.

industries.industry: Health insurers and health benefit plans
industries.note: The bill would have required every carrier and employer plan to cover the full federal preventive schedule and face an excise tax of up to 25 percent of premiums for failing to comply. Costs would likely have been passed into premiums, so insurers' interest in killing the bill ran against patients gaining guaranteed coverage.
Employer plans were directly covered by the mandate and tax, though 300 employers would have received grants for on-site wellness workshops, a partial offset.

industries.industry: Physicians, clinics, and preventive care providers
industries.note: Guaranteed coverage of preventive services across private plans, Medicare, Medicaid, veterans' care, and military dependent care would have meant more billable preventive visits.

The bill funded county clinics, dissemination of preventive health information, and on-site workshops on nutrition, smoking cessation, and stress management, directing federal money to these services.

industries.industry: Prescription drug manufacturers and other schedule consultants
industries.note: Representatives of drug manufacturers, chiropractors, and plan administrators were named as consultants in setting the national schedule, giving them a formal role in deciding which services every plan in the country had to cover.
